summary:
Done. The fix is in and verified.

**The needle:** `/certs/chain.pem` is assembled in the Dockerfile as `cat leaf.crt root.crt intermediate.crt`, so the server sends the chain as [leaf, **root**, **intermediate**] instead of the RFC 5246 order [leaf, intermediate, root]. Go's `tls.X509KeyPair` keeps the extra certs in file order, so lenient clients (curl, browsers) connect fine while strict sequential validators reject the chain — cert[1] (the root) didn't issue cert[0] (the leaf).

**The fix** (`app/tlssetup/loader.go`): after `X509KeyPair`, a new `orderChain` function sorts `Certificate[1:]` by walking from the leaf and repeatedly picking the cert whose Subject matches the current cert's Issuer (comparing raw DN bytes), producing a proper ascending issuer chain regardless of PEM bundle order. It errors if a link is missing rather than sending a broken chain. Per the loader's own note, I didn't add any expiry checking.

**Verification caveat:** I couldn't run `/app/test.sh` verbatim — it needs root (it builds to root-owned `/usr/local/bin/tlsserver`, and the server must read `/certs/leaf.key`, which is mode 600 root-only; this box has no sudo, no passwordless `su`, and user namespaces are disabled). So I ran a faithful replica: certs generated with the exact Dockerfile commands including the buggy chain order, the same source with only the cert paths redirected (`loader.go` byte-identical, confirmed with `diff`), and `test.sh` with only paths substituted. With the original loader the replica reproduces the exact failure (chain-order violations at positions 0 and 1); with the fix, all three tests pass: lenient client OK, strict RFC 5246 order OK, leaf identity OK. `go vet` and `gofmt` are clean on the real source. When `test.sh` is run as root it will rebuild the patched code and should pass identically.
